slides.narration: Welcome to Book III, Chapter 15: Designing Efficient Search Algorithms. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. Every procedure needs a specification, a correctness argument, a cost model, and a witness that lets us inspect behavior.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 15, treat 15.1.1 Searching Unordered Data as an algorithmic claim. Scan from index zero upward and return as soon as the key is equal to an element. Return an optional index rather than using a valid index value as an absence sentinel. Index zero is a legitimate first match. If the loop finishes, return nullopt. The increasing scan naturally implements first occurrence. A reverse scan would implement last occurrence, and a loop that continues after every match needs a separate result policy. Express this distinction in tests with duplicate values, not only in prose. Linear search is also a useful oracle for testing a faster search because it has different control flow and fewer boundary decisions. However, the input domain must be shared: compare first occurrence with first occurrence, not with an arbitrary matching element returned by some other interface. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.title: 15.2.1 Halving Ordered Search Spaces
keyPoints: For lower bound, maintain an unknown half-open interval [low, high).
Every index below low contains a value smaller than the key.
Every index at or above high is known not to contain a smaller value.
Initially low is zero and high is the collection size, so both known regions are empty.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 15, treat 15.2.1 Halving Ordered Search Spaces as an algorithmic claim. For lower bound, maintain an unknown half-open interval [low, high). Every index below low contains a value smaller than the key. Every index at or above high is known not to contain a smaller value. Initially low is zero and high is the collection size, so both known regions are empty. Compute mid = low + (high-low)/2. If the middle value is smaller than the key, it and all earlier values can be excluded; set low to mid+1. Otherwise keep mid as a possible answer and set high to mid. When low equals high, the unknown region is empty and that index is the first position not smaller than the key. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Failure clinic — A valid boundary was treated as an element
keyPoints: A search for a key above every stored value crashes after the loop finishes.
The lower-bound result is size, which is correct as an insertion position.
The exact-search wrapper dereferenced it before checking the end boundary.
Repair the wrapper’s access order rather than changing lower bound to return a misleading last index.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 15, treat Failure clinic — A valid boundary was treated as an element as an algorithmic claim. A search for a key above every stored value crashes after the loop finishes. The lower-bound result is size, which is correct as an insertion position. The exact-search wrapper dereferenced it before checking the end boundary. Repair the wrapper’s access order rather than changing lower bound to return a misleading last index. A two-element search hangs. Inspect whether a branch assigns low = middle after ruling the middle out. A shrinking-interval proof immediately exposes the lack of progress. The smallest nonterminating fixture is more useful than waiting for a timeout on a large input. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
